The `@wordpress/ui` `Button` component does not provide visual feedback specific to the pressed state. `:hover`, `:active`, and `:focus` all share the same styles, so clicking a button looks the same as hovering it. There is no clear “pressed” moment before the click completes.

## Current behavior

In `packages/ui/src/button/style.module.css`, interactive states are grouped:

```css
&:not([data-disabled]):is(:hover, :active, :focus) {
	background-color: var(--wp-ui-button-background-color-active);
	color: var(--wp-ui-button-foreground-color-active);
	border-color: var(--wp-ui-button-border-color-active);
}
```

The `-active` custom properties map to design tokens whose descriptions also combine hover, focus, and pressed (e.g. `--wpds-color-bg-interactive-brand-strong-active`: “hovered, focused, or active”). So the component and tokens treat “active” as one state, not a separate pressed state.

In Storybook, click and hold a button: it should look different from hover alone, but today it does not.

## Why this matters

1. Buttons should respond at the moment of interaction, not only on hover. Without distinct `:active` styling, clicks can feel unresponsive, especially on touch devices where hover is absent and press is the main cue.
2. Hover is exploratory (“what happens if I click?”). Press is commitment (“I am clicking now”). Using the same styles for both removes an important layer of feedback and makes the UI feel flat.
3. The legacy `Button` in `@wordpress/components` does distinguish `:active` from `:hover` — for example, primary buttons use a darker background on press (`$components-color-accent-darker-20`) than on hover (`$components-color-accent-darker-10`). As `@wordpress/ui` replaces `@wordpress/components`, we risk regressing a behavior users already expect.
4. Gutenberg relies heavily on buttons in toolbars, inspectors, and dialogs. In those contexts, subtle but reliable press feedback helps users trust that their action registered. Especially for icon-only and compact buttons where color change alone may be hard to notice.
5. The token docs define an `active` state as “hovered, pressed, or selected.” That works for token naming, but components still need to decide how to map CSS pseudo-classes. `Button` currently collapses them entirely; we should decide intentionally whether pressed needs its own token(s), or some other treatment.

## Possible directions
* Add new color tokens and mimic `Button` in `@wordpress/components`.
  * If we do this we should ensure all button variants include `:active` styles that differ from hover and focus.
* A non-color based approach, e.g. a subtle scale animation.
* Something else?
resources.title: `@wordpress/ui` Button lacks distinct `:active` (pressed) styling

## What problem does this address?

Currently, button styles are such that the focus outline is removed while pressing the control (while the button is activated).

This can be problematic for a few reasons:

- There is no indication that the button is focused while the button is activated. And, in general, it's unintuitive that a button style effect would be removed in response to its activation.
- This is not entirely consistent with how it behaves in the rest of the WordPress admin, which sometimes retains the focus while while active (though this is not entirely consistent, see [related Slack discussion](https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RP4X03/p1791225739029399)).
- To my knowledge, there's not much precedent for this being a typical behavior in UI interaction design.

## What is your proposed solution?

We should devise a single, unified approach for handling focused-while-active button styles, and apply it consistently across Gutenberg and WordPress Core.

In practical terms, this could include one or more of:

- Removing the styles that hide the focus ring while active
- Substitute intended effect of click-activation focus styling to avoid distracting focus rings while clicked (e.g. using `:focus-active`)

While `:focus-active` is intended to be a modern solution to handling styles that should be differentiated by input method, it has some hazards, including those [raised by @joedolson in Slack](https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RP4X03/p1791227305220449?thread_ts=1791225739.029399&cid=C02RP4X03):

> The main concerns with :focus-visible is that it loses some valuable cues for low vision and cognitive support AT which uses pointers to track active position in a document, and can create disorientation for users using mixed-input - jumping between mouse and keyboard. Screen reader browse modes can break this, as well, which is a problem for low vision users who use screen readers for support.

> Voice command is another tricky heuristic to detect - it's neither a pointer nor a keyboard action, and can cause users to struggle with indicators.

Since this issue applies within the context of Gutenberg, any decisions that result in styling changes should be accompanied by a corresponding Trac ticket.

### Description

Historically, npm dist-tags provided a convenient way to determine which versions of @wordpress/* packages corresponded to a given WordPress Core release.

Since WordPress Core no longer consumes packages directly from npm (https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/64393), this mapping is no longer available. While this does not affect Core itself, it creates challenges for downstream consumers that rely on the information to align their tooling with the APIs that are actually available in a specific WordPress release.

### Use cases

#### TypeScript compatibility

Many projects install @wordpress/* packages primarily for TypeScript types while relying on the externalized versions shipped by WordPress at runtime.

Using the latest npm packages can expose types for APIs that have not yet shipped in a given WordPress release, leading to inaccurate editor hints, false assumptions about API availability, and compatibility issues.

A mapping between WordPress releases and package versions allows consumers to install package versions that accurately reflect the runtime environment.

#### Automated testing

Projects may run unit and integration tests against different WordPress versions to verify compatibility across the supported range.

To accurately reproduce a given WordPress environment, it is helpful to know which versions of the @wordpress/* packages correspond to a specific WordPress release. Without a programmatic mapping, test environments may end up using package versions that differ from those actually available in WordPress, reducing confidence in test results and making compatibility verification more difficult.

### Additional context

Discussion in Slack:
https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02QB2JS7/p1780499303839469

## Start here

Two ways in, depending on why you're here:

- **Want to try it?** Jump to [Testing](https://playground.wordpress.net/gutenberg.html?pr=78994) - it runs in Playground, nothing to install.
- **Here to review the code?** Jump to [Reviewing the stack](#reviewing-the-stack) - start at the bottom, #80427.

## What problem does this address?

As Notes evolve beyond simple block-level comments, this enhancement adds support for suggested edits that can be applied directly to the content. This is similar to the "Suggesting" workflow in Google Docs, where reviewers propose changes and authors can accept or reject them.

While this started as a Notes concept, it is more broadly an editorial workflow / content editing concept that overlaps with how Notes work.

## What is the solution?

In **Suggest mode**, edits are not applied to the content directly. Instead they are captured as suggestions rendered in context, which the post author can accept or reject. There are two kinds of suggestion:

- **Inline text suggestions** - typing, deletion, cut, paste, and formatting (bold / italic / link) toggles within rich text.
- **Structural suggestions** - block-level changes such as inserting, removing, or moving blocks, and attribute changes like heading level or alignment.

### Design: inline suggestions are markers, by construction

Every inline edit becomes a `<mark class="wp-suggestion">` marker **by construction**, so no edit falls back to a separate overlay diff render. This follows the Google Docs model - the text shows once and is styled in place, rather than showing paired `<del>`/`<ins>` runs.

- **Text edits** - typing, word/line deletion, cut, and single-line paste are caught on `beforeinput` / `cut` / `paste` by the suggestion keyboards, which write markers directly. The remaining `onChange` seams (committed IME composition, autocorrect, drag-drop, multi-line paste) are diffed into markers by a singleton content reconciler.
- **Formatting** - bold / italic / link toggles become a single `format`-type marker wrapping the run.

The result is a single accept/reject path and a single serialization. An attribute-only revert shim on the overlay remains **only** for structural attribute changes (heading level, alignment); it never touches inline text or formatting.

A safety-net e2e asserts the invariant directly: a block never carries both an inline marker and an overlay diff.

## Testing

#78994 bundles all nine layers into one branch and builds it in Playground, so there is nothing to install. It is also the one place the feature is **enabled by default** - everywhere else it sits behind an experiment, off until you turn it on:

[![Test in WordPress Playground](https://img.shields.io/badge/Test_in-WP_Playground-blue?style=for-the-badge&logo=wordpress)](https://playground.wordpress.net/gutenberg.html?pr=78994)

https://playground.wordpress.net/gutenberg.html?pr=78994

**Setup:** none. Open a post with a few paragraphs and look for **Options (⋮) > Mode**. A multi-paragraph post matters - some of the input handling only shows up once there is more than one block.

(If you are testing one of the stack PRs instead of #78994, enable **Settings > Experiments > Collaboration > Suggestion Mode** first. #78994 is the only branch that skips that step.)

### 1. Switching modes

- **Options (⋮) > Mode** offers **Editing**, **Suggesting**, and **Viewing**. Switching announces itself with a snackbar ("You're suggesting").
- **Viewing** is read-only: you can select and scroll, but not type.
- Keyboard shortcuts follow the Google Docs convention: `⇧⌥⌘Z` / `⇧⌥⌘X` / `⇧⌥⌘C` on Mac, `Ctrl+Shift+Alt` with the same letters elsewhere. They register wherever Suggest mode is available.
- Reload the editor - the mode returns to **Editing**. It is session-scoped on purpose and never persisted.

Switch to **Suggesting** for everything below.

### 2. Inline text suggestions

- **Type** in the middle of a paragraph → the new text appears as an underlined add marker, and one "Add: …" note appears in the sidebar (not "Format:").
- **Delete** three ways: select text and press Delete; press Backspace at a caret (repeating grows one marker rather than one per keystroke); use word-delete (Option/Ctrl+Backspace). Each becomes a struck-through del marker - the text stays until accepted.
- **Cut** (Cmd/Ctrl+X) a selection → del marker, and the clipboard still receives the cut text.
- **Type over** a selection → a del + add pair (two notes).
- **Paste** a single line → one add marker. Paste multiple lines → captured as a whole-attribute suggestion, never a raw commit.
- **Autocorrect / spellcheck replace / IME commit** → reconciled into add/del markers.
- **Grapheme safety:** backspace over emoji/ZWJ sequences (👨‍👩‍👧, flags) marks whole graphemes.
- Edits that straddle an existing marker are left alone rather than corrupting another suggestion.

### 3. Formatting suggestions

- Select a run and toggle **bold / italic / link** → the run is wrapped in a single format marker (dotted underline, no duplicated text). The note records the original so Reject can restore it.

### 4. Structural suggestions

- **Insert** a block and type into it → ONE "Insert block" note (no extra "Add" note); the block carries the pending-insert treatment. An empty inserted block does not suggest anything until it has content.
- **Delete** a block → it stays visible with a struck-through pending-remove treatment.
- **Move** a block up/down → it lands at the proposed position with a pending-move treatment and a non-interactive ghost marks its origin. Moving the same block twice keeps a single note.
- **Change an attribute** (heading level via the block switcher, alignment) → captured as an attribute suggestion.

### 5. Notes sidebar

- Every suggestion appears as a note with a Docs-style summary ("Add:", "Delete:", "Format:", "Insert block:", "Move block:", "Remove block:").
- If a non-notes sidebar (eg. post/block settings) is open when a suggestion is created, it switches to **All notes** automatically so the note is immediately visible; a closed sidebar stays closed.
- With multiple suggesters, markers and pending treatments are tinted per author, taken from their avatar color.

### 6. Undo

- Undo a just-typed addition → the marker and its note both go away.
- Same for a deletion, a type-over (both notes go), a format change, and each structural type.
- Make several suggestions and undo repeatedly → they withdraw newest-first. Redo must not crash.

### 7. Persistence and saving

- **Save draft stays available** while suggestions are pending (structural pending state saves into content and is hidden from the front end at render time).
- After saving, there is **no** "unsaved changes" browser warning.
- **Reload** the post → inline markers, pending structural treatments (including the move ghost), and their notes all survive, and can still be accepted or rejected.

### 8. Review cycle (as the author, in Editing intent)

- **Accept** one of each kind: addition (text kept, marker unwrapped), deletion (text removed), format (proposed formatting kept), insert (block kept), remove (block removed), move (new order kept, ghost cleared), attribute (change lands in content).
- **Reject** one of each kind: the content reverts exactly (a rejected move restores the original order, including after a reload).
- Accepting or rejecting shows a "Suggestion applied." / "Suggestion rejected." snackbar.
- **Front end:** publish/preview with pending suggestions → proposed additions and inserted blocks never render until accepted; pending deletions and format runs still render their real text.

If you hit something that does not match the above, please note which step and which mode you were in - that narrows it down a lot.

## Reviewing the stack

![Suggest mode review stack](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adamsilverstein/gutenberg/issue-assets/issue-assets/suggest-stack-9pr.svg)

- [ ] #80427 - editor intent + experiment gate (36 files)
- [ ] #80428 - suggestion storage, REST controller, provider (15 files)
- [ ] #80429 - block-level capture, attribute and structural (20 files)
- [ ] #80430 - inline marker primitive (17 files)
- [ ] #80431 - inline suggestion operations (15 files)
- [ ] #80432 - review UI, Apply / Reject sidebar and summary (10 files)
- [ ] #80433 - inline live wiring (61 files)
- [ ] #82047 - architecture documentation (4 files)
- [ ] #82048 - end-to-end test suite (16 files)

### How to review this

**Start at the bottom and work up.** Each PR targets the one below it rather than `trunk`, so its diff shows only its own layer. Reading #80427 first and moving up means you never see the same code twice, and each layer arrives with its dependencies already in place.

**Review each PR against its own base.** GitHub's diff already does this - resist comparing against `trunk`, which will show you the whole feature every time.

**Leave comments on the PR that owns the code.** If something in #80431 looks wrong because of a decision made in #80429, the comment belongs on #80429.

**A few files are deliberately split across layers**, so they look incomplete when you first meet them:

- `with-suggestion-overlay.tsx` - lands in #80429 with attribute and structural capture; #80433 restores the inline handoff.
- `provider.ts` - lands in #80428 with attribute/structural apply and reject; #80433 restores the inline apply/reject.
- `store-interceptor.ts` - lands in #80429; #80433 adds the inline content-edit planning.
- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.1/block-suggestions.php` - meta registration in #80428, the structural strip in #80429, the inline marker strip in #80433.

Everything else is whole in exactly one PR.

**Follow up fixes live in the layer that owns the code.** The review round that produced #81655-#81695 originally merged everything onto the top of the stack, which left #80433 at 115 files and put fixes to List View, post status and the intent switcher three layers above the code they change. Those now sit in their own layer, and the documentation and the end-to-end suite have their own PRs, so each layer reviews as one kind of thing.

**If you only have time for a slice:** #80429 (block-level capture) and #80431 (inline suggestion operations) hold most of the interesting logic. #80427 is the smallest and a good place to sanity-check the gating approach.

**Test while you review** - #78994 builds the tip of the stack, so the [Testing](#testing) walkthrough above exercises exactly the code you are reading. Its only departure is that it turns the feature on by default; the experiment gate itself is reviewed on #80427.

Architecture write-up: `docs/explanations/architecture/suggestions.md`.

### Automated coverage

- **Unit:** the `suggestion-mode`, `inline-suggestions` (diff/plan engines), `inline-markers`, and `attribute-suggestions` suites.
- **E2E:** 64 tests - `suggestion-mode.spec.js` golden paths (22), `suggestion-mode-review.spec.js` review cycle (19), `suggestion-mode-undo.spec.js` (9), `suggestion-mode-overlay-retirement.spec.js` safety net (8: the invariant plus the word-delete / cut / multi-line-paste / autocorrect / IME seams), and `suggestion-mode-persistence.spec.js` (6: save/reload round-trips and the front-end strip).
- **PHP:** the front-end strips are covered by the `strip-inline-suggestion-markers` and `strip-pending-structural-suggestions` phpunit tests.

<details>
<summary>Superseded earlier stacks</summary>

The feature was originally prototyped across a larger multi-workstream stack (#77403, #77404, #77405, #77406, #78351, #78352, #78353, #78308, #77967, #77968, #77970, #77971, #77973, #77978, #77979, #78412, #79282) plus the combined testing branch (#78994). A visual stack diagram of the original layout is in [this comment](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/73411#issuecomment-4845842515).

That work was then consolidated into a manually stacked two-PR series - #79713 (core subsystem + experiment gate) and #79714 (inline markers; #79752, overlay retirement, was folded into it). Those two PRs are now closed, reworked into the finer-grained seven-PR stack above with identical end-state code.

</details>

## Open questions

1. Should suggestions be tied to a specific version or revision of the post?
2. How should conflicts be handled if content changes before a suggestion is applied (concurrent / multi-author suggestions)?

### Description

When `wp-env reset` cannot reset the database, it still reports that the environment was reset and exits with code `0`. The database is left as it was, and WordPress is not reconfigured.

I expect `wp-env reset` to report the failure and exit with a non-zero code, so a failed reset is noticed, both when run by hand and in scripts or CI.

The reset runs `wp db reset --yes` in the `cli` (and `tests-cli`) container, then reconfigures WordPress. In the Docker runtime's `clean()`, each environment's chain ends in `.catch( () => {} )`, which discards any error:

https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/1a6c8ab43bdc71421d8fbd595a200a61f9541581/packages/env/lib/runtime/docker/index.js#L517-L519

https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/1a6c8ab43bdc71421d8fbd595a200a61f9541581/packages/env/lib/runtime/docker/index.js#L528-L530

This came up in #83751, where `wp db reset` failed against MariaDB versions before 11.4 (the MariaDB 11.4+ client in the CLI image requires TLS), and `wp-env reset` reported success without resetting anything. #83751 addresses that cause, but any other failure of `wp db reset` is still hidden.

### Step-by-step reproduction instructions

1. In an empty directory, create a `.wp-env.json` with `{ "testsEnvironment": false }` and run `wp-env start`.
2. Create a post: `wp-env run cli wp post create --post_title=marker-post --post_status=publish`.
3. Make `wp db reset` fail by giving WP-CLI a wrong database password: `wp-env run cli wp config set DB_PASSWORD wrong-password`.
4. Run `wp-env reset development`, then `echo $?`.
5. Restore the password: `wp-env run cli wp config set DB_PASSWORD password`.
6. List the posts: `wp-env run cli wp post list --fields=ID,post_title`.

Step 4 prints `✔ Reset development environment.` and the exit code is `0`. Step 6 still lists `marker-post`, so the database was not reset.

Land an initial version of the `data-wp-html` directive and a reactive navigation lifecycle for the Interactivity API router in WordPress 7.2.

The `data-wp-html` directive will add a missing primitive: today there is no supported way to render markup from the store inside an interactive region and have the result reflected reactively. This initial version will ship a directive that renders only values explicitly trusted by application code through `asDangerousHTML()`, leaving sanitized plain strings for a later version. Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
Currently, the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) lacks a native way to search for specific text or patterns across all blocks within a post or page. Users who need to perform bulk changes (e.g., changing a specific brand name, a recurring typo, or updating a specific term) must manually find and edit each block one by one. This is time-consuming and prone to human error, especially in long-form content.

Describe the solution you’d like
I would like to see a native “Find and Replace” tool integrated into the Block Editor interface.

Proposed Workflow:

Access: A new option in the “Options” (three dots) menu or a keyboard shortcut (e.g., Ctrl+F or Cmd+F specifically for the editor context).
Interface: A small, non-intrusive search bar/panel appearing at the top or side of the editor.
Functionality:
Find: Search for a string of text within all blocks.
Replace: A field to input the new text to replace the found string.
Scope: Options to “Replace One” or “Replace All”.
Case Sensitivity: Options for case-sensitive or whole-word matching.
Highlighting: Highlighting the matches within the editor view before applying the replacement.
Describe alternatives you’ve considered
Currently, users must rely on third-party plugins (like “Better Search Replace” for database-wide changes) or manually editing blocks. However, these are often overkill for a single post or can be risky if used incorrectly on the entire database. A lightweight, editor-level tool would be much safer and more efficient for content creators.

Additional context

Having this feature natively would significantly improve the user experience for content editors and power users, bringing the Block Editor closer to the standards of modern word processors and other advanced CMS editors

## What?

See https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/discussions/82492, where @nickchomey suggested using an asm.js build of `es-module-lexer`.

Client-side navigation can now load new script modules under a Content Security Policy without `'unsafe-eval'` or `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`.

## Why?

The FAQ says that the Interactivity API works with any custom Content Security Policy, but under a policy without `'unsafe-eval'`, navigating to a page with script modules that aren't loaded yet falls back to a full page reload. The default build of `es-module-lexer`, which the router uses to rewrite module imports, compiles WebAssembly and decodes module specifiers with `eval()`. Without `'unsafe-eval'`, the loader fails, `fetchPage()` swallows the error and `navigate()` reloads the page. `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` alone isn't enough.

## How?

-   `loader.ts` imports `parse()` from `es-module-lexer/js`: the same lexer compiled to asm.js, without WebAssembly or `eval()`. It only exports `parse()`, so the `initPromise` plumbing is gone.
-   `es-module-lexer` is now `^1.7.0`, the version the lockfile already resolves. The `./js` export only ships types since 1.6.0.
-   The FAQ explains what a policy needs for client-side navigation: nonces with `'strict-dynamic'`, or `blob:` in `script-src`.
-   New unit and e2e tests, and a test plugin that sends the policies.

Notes:

-   Both builds return identical results for 4,774 ESM files. The router bundle grows from 26.4 KB to 32.4 KB, but shrinks from 11.8 KB to 11.6 KB gzipped. Parsing takes about 0.05 ms per small module instead of 0.03 ms, and the asm.js build allocates a 1 MiB buffer the first time it parses.
-   After this change, no Interactivity API script module contains `eval`, `Function(` or `WebAssembly`. The nonce policy in the tests is the [strict CSP that web.dev recommends](https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp), so sites don't have to weaken their policy.
-   Alternatives: `es-module-lexer/minimal/js` needs a major update to 2.3 or later, and keeping WebAssembly with an asm.js fallback would ship both builds and still report violations.
-   No public API changes, and esbuild, webpack and TypeScript consumers keep working. The CommonJS build now requires an ESM-only module, as `@wordpress/blocks` already does with `uuid` and `marked`.
-   Backports: the commit has small conflicts on `wp/7.1` and `wp/7.0`, where the unit test also needs porting to Jest. `wp/7.0` needs `es-module-lexer@1.7.0` in its lockfile. WordPress 6.9 needs an npm release on the `wp-6.9` dist-tag.

## Testing Instructions

-   `npm run test:unit -- packages/interactivity-router`: preloads modules with `eval()` and WebAssembly blocked. Fails on trunk.
-   `npm run test:e2e -- test/e2e/specs/interactivity/router-script-modules.spec.ts`: navigates to pages with new script modules under a nonce policy and an allowlist policy, sent by the new Gutenberg Test Content Security Policy plugin, and checks that the navigation stays client-side without `eval`, `wasm-eval` or script `blob:` violations.

Manually:

1. Activate the Gutenberg Test Content Security Policy and Gutenberg Test Interactive Blocks plugins.
2. Create the posts with the `test/router-script-modules-*` blocks as the e2e test does, and open the post that links to the others with `?csp=nonce` added to its URL.
3. Follow the links and press the Static and Dynamic buttons. On trunk, the first link reloads the page. With this change, the navigation stays client-side and the browser reports no Content Security Policy violations.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

None, this doesn't change the UI.

## What?

Two follow-ups to #80578, which is what actually removes the spotlight from the notes flows. Stacked on that branch - please merge #80578 first.

Related: #72860

## Why?

#80578 is approved and thorough about the new markings, but two loose ends came out of reviewing it against the original issue:

1. **Nothing asserts the absence of the dimming.** The e2e suite covers the tint, the underline and its thickening in detail, and none of it would fail if the spotlight came back tomorrow. That fade is the whole complaint in #72860, so it deserves its own guard.
2. **The spotlight plumbing is now dead.** Once #80578 lands, `toggleBlockSpotlight` has no dispatchers anywhere, so the reducer it feeds can never leave its null state.

## How?

**The e2e guard.** A new `Canvas dimming` block in `block-notes.spec.js` with two tests: selecting a note from the sidebar, and opening the add-note form. Both read the class that switches the fade on (`is-focus-mode` on the block list root) together with the `opacity` an unrelated block actually computes to, so the test still fails if the fade is ever moved onto a different hook. The add-note case gets its own test because #72870 spotlighted the composer separately from note selection.

The noted paragraph is deliberately the second of two, so the block a spotlight would fade is the one above it - which is the case desrosj and joedolson both raised, a note saying "move this before the previous one" being unreadable when the previous one is dimmed.

**The dead code.** Removes the `toggleBlockSpotlight` action, the `hasBlockSpotlight` reducer, and its registration in the combined reducer. What was left of the `hasBlockSpotlight` selector is then exactly the `editedContentOnlySection` check that `BlockList` already reads on the line below it, so this inlines that instead of keeping a private selector that only restates one field. All private API, no deprecation needed.

`.is-focus-mode` and its CSS stay: the user's Spotlight mode preference and content-only section editing both still use them. The only thing removed is the notes path into it.

## Testing Instructions

[![Test with WordPress Playground](https://img.shields.io/badge/Test%20with-WordPress%20Playground-3858E9?logo=wordpress&logoColor=white)](https://playground.wordpress.net/gutenberg.html?pr=81538)

Enable notes, then in the post editor:

1. Add two paragraphs, note the second one. Select the note in the sidebar - the first paragraph stays fully readable, and the noted one is marked by its outline.
2. Turn on Spotlight mode (Options > Spotlight mode) and click around with no notes involved. The dimming still works exactly as before.
3. Edit a content-only section in a template - the rest of the canvas still dims.

### Automated

- `npm run test:e2e -- test/e2e/specs/editor/various/block-notes.spec.js`
- `npm run test:unit packages/block-editor/src/store` - 637 passing, no test referenced the removed state.

## Notes for reviewers

The plan for #72860 also floated an e2e test that flips the real `focusMode` preference on and off to prove notes leave it alone. That one is left out on purpose: the preference persists to the database, and `block-notes.spec.js` leaving persisted preferences behind has already been implicated in unrelated specs failing. Point 2 of the manual steps above covers the same ground without the shared state.

## What?
`ContentEditableControl` keeps a disabled field focusable (`tabIndex="-1"`, still `aria-disabled` and not `contentEditable`). The notes form uses that to disable its field while a note or reply is being sent. Today the field accepts typing during the request; text typed then is silently kept in the field after a reply, or dropped when the new-note form closes.

## Why?
`NoteForm` applied `isSubmitting` to the submit button only, and compensated for the open field with a "keep anything typed since" check after the save. Disabling the field is the right fix, but a focused `contentEditable` that stops being editable loses focus to `body` in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and nothing restores it after a reply or a failed save. Keeping the disabled field focusable removes that focus loss at the source instead of adding refocus logic to the form.

## How?
- `ContentEditableControl`: `tabIndex={ disabled ? -1 : undefined }` next to `contentEditable={ ! disabled }`. The field stays out of the Tab order but keeps focus when disabled while focused, like `Button` with `accessibleWhenDisabled`. Private API; consumers are the validated wrapper and the notes `RichTextControl`.
- `NoteForm`: `disabled={ isSubmitting }` on the field and an unconditional reset after a successful save; the stale-text guard goes away.

## Testing Instructions
1. Open a post, add a paragraph, choose "Add note" from the block options menu.
2. Throttle the network in dev tools (Slow 3G), type a note, press Cmd+Enter. The field appears disabled and ignores typing until the note appears; then focus lands on the new thread.
3. Click the thread, type a reply, press Cmd+Enter. The field is disabled during the request, then cleared, with focus still in it.
4. Block the comments request in dev tools (right-click the `wp/v2/comments` POST, Block request URL) and submit another reply. The error snackbar appears, the text stays, and focus stays in the field.

## What?

Combines three in-flight notes-highlighting PRs into one, per [feedback on #80493](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/80493#issuecomment-5048059519). They all change how a note marks its place in the canvas, and the result only makes sense reviewed together:

- #80493 - keep the block outline, drop the spotlight dimming on note selection
- #80498 - highlight the whole text block for block-level notes
- #80544 - hold the tint at one low alpha, emphasize with an underline (fixes #80543)

Those three stay open for now and can be closed in favor of this one.

Fixes #72860.
Fixes #80543.

## Why?

Each PR was solving a piece of the same problem, and the pieces conflicted:

- #80498 tinted a whole block at 0x40, deepening to 0x80 when selected.
- #80544 removed exactly that deepening for inline markers, because the tint sits *behind* the text: every increment is subtracted from whatever contrast the theme provides, and the composited result can't be measured from CSS since the canvas background comes from `theme.json`.
- #80493 removed the spotlight, which is what the "selected" state used to lean on.

Landing them separately would have shipped an intermediate state nobody wants to see, and left the last one to unpick the first two.

## How?

One consistent model, with a marking that is visible **at rest** in every case:

| | Rest | Hover / focus / selected |
|---|---|---|
| Inline marker | author tint @ 0x40 + underline on its words | underline thickens to 3px |
| Block-level note | author tint @ 0x40 + rule along the block's bottom edge | + the block's own outline |
| Whole canvas | untouched | untouched (no dimming) |

The resting indicator is the point, and it is what lets the spotlight go: with nothing shown at rest, removing the dimming would leave no connection between a note in the sidebar and its place in the canvas, which is [@jasmussen's central objection](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/80498#issuecomment-5043524040).

The tint alpha is a single constant with no per-state variant anywhere, guarded by a unit test in both builders. Emphasis is only ever a silhouette change - a thicker rule - so marking a note costs the theme's text contrast one fixed amount and never more, which is the [#80543](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/80543) constraint.

Two details worth reviewing:

- **The block-level rule sits under the block, not under each line.** A wrapped paragraph striped on every line reads as formatting, where a single bottom edge reads as a boundary. For single-line blocks (list items, headings) the two are identical, which is the case the mockups show. It is an inset `box-shadow` rather than a `border` so adding it cannot reflow the canvas.
- **Selection emphasis for block-level notes is the block outline**, since thickening a rule that spans a whole paragraph is much louder than doing the same to a few words.

Per [@jasmussen's feedback on #80544](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/80544#issuecomment-5043139186), every rule is `color-mix(in srgb, <author color> 30%, currentColor)` at `1.5px`. The canvas can be light or dark while the palette is fixed, so anchoring to the text color is what keeps the stroke above the 3:1 non-text contrast minimum in both, with as much author hue as fits underneath it; the fixed pixel thickness keeps it distinct from a hyperlink at body size without becoming a bar under a heading.

Incidentally this also resolves the dimming [@noruzzamans noticed while testing #80544](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/80544#issuecomment-5042259172) - that was the spotlight, which #80493 removes.

## Testing Instructions

[![Test with WordPress Playground](https://img.shields.io/badge/Test%20with-WordPress%20Playground-3858E9?logo=wordpress&logoColor=white)](https://playground.wordpress.net/gutenberg.html?pr=80578)

Enable notes, then in the post editor:

1. **Block-level note.** Select a paragraph without selecting any text, add a note. Click away so nothing is selected: the paragraph stays tinted with a rule along its bottom edge. Select the note in the sidebar and the block picks up its outline, with the tint no stronger than before.
2. **Inline note.** Select a few words, add a note. Click away: those words stay tinted and underlined. Hover the marker, or select the note from the sidebar, and the underline thickens - the tint behind the words does not deepen.
3. **No spotlight.** With a note selected, the rest of the canvas stays at full contrast - nothing dims.
4. Try both in a dark theme, and with several authors' notes on one page.

### Automated

- `npm run test:unit packages/editor/src/components/collab-sidebar` - 19 tests over the two CSS builders, including guards that the marking is present on the resting rule, that neither builder can reintroduce a per-state alpha, and that the rule color never resolves to the raw palette value.
- `npm run test:e2e -- test/e2e/specs/editor/various/block-notes.spec.js` - 49 passing locally, covering the resting underline and its thickening on selection, the block's resting bottom rule, the computed mix against the theme's text color, and the tint holding steady across states.

## Screenshots or screencast

## What?
See #83751.

Makes the unit test workflow's "Docker container debug information" step check which database client the `mysql` container has, instead of always running `mariadb --version`.

## Why?
#83751 adds a `mariadbVersion` option and a `WP_ENV_MARIADB_VERSION` environment variable, so `wp-env` can run older MariaDB versions, including ones older than 10.4. Which client those versions ship depends on the version: MariaDB 10.4.5 and earlier only have `mysql`, 10.4.6 to 10.11 have both, and 11.0 and later only have `mariadb`. If this workflow ever runs against a version older than 10.4.6, the step fails with `mariadb: not found` and stops the PHP test jobs before PHPUnit runs.

#83751 already handles the same naming difference in its database health check, where it picks `mariadb-admin` or `mysqladmin`. This does the same for the debug step.

## How?
The step runs a short `sh -c` script in the `mysql` container: `mariadb --version` when the `mariadb` command exists, otherwise `mysql --version`. The `--` before `sh` passes the script to the container without `wp-env` parsing it. On the current `mariadb:lts` image, the output is unchanged.

The same command is already used in the `wp/7.1`–`wp/6.2` branch repair PRs (for example #83831), where it passes in CI.

## Testing Instructions
1. In CI, the "Docker container debug information" step in the PHP jobs passes and prints the MariaDB version, as before.
2. The script was run directly in the official images. It runs `mysql --version` on MariaDB 10.2, 10.3 and 10.4.5, `mariadb --version` on 10.4.6, 10.11, 11.0 and 13.0.2, and `mysql --version` on MySQL 5.7 and 8.0, exiting with 0 every time. To try it with a single version:
   ```
   docker run --rm --entrypoint sh mariadb:10.3 -c 'if command -v mariadb > /dev/null; then mariadb --version; else mysql --version; fi'
   ```
3. Optionally, with #83751 applied, set `"mariadbVersion": "10.3"` in `.wp-env.test.json`, run `npm run wp-env-test start`, then run the step's first command.

## What?

Adds a `mariadbVersion` option to `.wp-env.json` and a `WP_ENV_MARIADB_VERSION` environment variable, so the MariaDB version used by the Docker runtime can be chosen. Accepted values are `"lts"`, `"latest"`, or a numeric version such as `"10.11"` or `"11.4.2"`. Leaving it unset (or `null`) keeps today's `mariadb:lts`.

## Why?

The database image is currently hardcoded to `mariadb:lts`, while the PHP version can already be set with `phpVersion` / `WP_ENV_PHP_VERSION`. Projects that test against older WordPress releases need to pin a MariaDB version those releases support. In this repository, that means pinning the newest compatible MariaDB on each `wp/X.Y` branch, so this change is kept small and follows the existing `phpVersion` pattern to make backporting straightforward.

This is also important for maintaining older versions of WordPress, allowing tests to be run only on versions of MariaDB that a given `wp/X.Y` branch actually supported (see #82780).

## How?

- `mariadbVersion` is parsed exactly like `phpVersion`: at the root or per environment (`env.development`, `env.tests`), with `WP_ENV_MARIADB_VERSION` overriding every environment. `checkMariaDBVersion()` accepts `lts`, `latest` or a version number, and rejects anything else (`LTS`, `11-noble`, `lts-10`, non-strings).
- The accepted tags, the `lts` default and the image name live in `db-env.js`, and each database service uses its own environment's value: `mariadb:<version>`, defaulting to `mariadb:lts`.
- Every version uses one health check, which checks the image at runtime instead of guessing from the version: it runs `healthcheck.sh --connect --innodb_initialized` when the data directory has the healthcheck user's `.my-healthcheck.cnf` and the image has the script, and otherwise pings the server over TCP on `127.0.0.1` with `mariadb-admin` (11.0+ only ships this name) or `mysqladmin` (versions before 10.4 only ship this name). `healthcheck.sh` was added to the images in 2022 and the healthcheck user in 2023, older tags were never rebuilt, and images such as the final 10.2 and 10.3 builds ship the script without the user. Both are checked because the file lives in the data volume and the script in the image, so an older image (for example `10.6.4` after `10.6`) can find a file a newer one left behind. The `lts` and `latest` images always have both, so they run the same `healthcheck.sh` check as before.
- MariaDB cannot downgrade to an older major or minor version. When `wp-env start` fails and a database container exited with an error, it reads the newest version recorded in that database's data directory and the image's version. If the data is from a newer major or minor version (for example, after switching from a branch on `lts` to one pinned to `10.6` in the same checkout), it stops with an error naming both versions and how to resolve it. The data is left untouched. Failures with other causes, such as a port already in use, keep their own error.
- When pulling images fails, `wp-env start` checks whether each image it pulls is available locally. If one is not, such as a `mariadbVersion` that does not exist, it stops with an error naming the image and pointing to `mariadbVersion`, instead of reporting that cached images will be used. When every image is cached, such as offline, it continues as before.
- The MariaDB client in the `wordpress:cli` images (11.4 and later) requires TLS, which MariaDB servers before 11.4 do not offer, so `wp db` commands, and `wp-env reset`, which runs `wp db reset`, failed against a pinned older version. WP-CLI 2.12 runs the client with `--no-defaults`, so a client option file cannot change this. The CLI image now wraps each MariaDB client to add `--skip-ssl-verify-server-cert`, which lets the client fall back to an unencrypted connection when the server has no TLS. That is the same flag WP-CLI adds from db-command 3.0, so the wrappers can be removed once a WP-CLI release with it is in the image.
- `checkVersion()` (`phpVersion`, `WP_ENV_PHP_VERSION`) now uses the same anchored version pattern as `checkMariaDBVersion()` and the JSON schema. Previously it only required a digit somewhere in the value, so values such as `8.2-apache` or `abc8` passed and then failed because no matching `wordpress:cli-php` image exists. They are now rejected with a validation error.
- The `MYSQL_*` service environment variables are unchanged. Older images only understand those names.
- The option is added to `schemas/json/wp-env.json`, and the README documents it, including running `wp-env cleanup` before switching to a lower version and emulation for 5.5 on Apple silicon. The Playground runtime (SQLite) ignores it.

Existing configurations use the same image as before. The health check command itself changes, but for the default `lts` image it runs the same `healthcheck.sh` check.

## Testing Instructions

1. In a directory with a `.wp-env.json` such as `{ "plugins": [], "mariadbVersion": "10.6.4" }`, run `wp-env start` using this branch's `packages/env/bin/wp-env`.
2. Run `docker ps` and confirm the `mysql` container uses `mariadb:10.6.4` and reports `(healthy)`.
3. Run `wp-env run cli wp core is-installed` and `wp-env run cli wp db check`, and confirm both succeed. Create a post, run `wp-env reset development`, and confirm the post is gone.
4. Run `wp-env cleanup`, then repeat with `"lts"`, `"latest"`, `"10.3"`, `"10.11"`, `"5.5"` (on Apple silicon, set `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64` for 5.5), and with no `mariadbVersion` at all.
5. Start with `"lts"`, then change `mariadbVersion` to `"10.6"` and run `wp-env start` again. It should stop with an error saying the database was last used by a newer MariaDB version. Change it back to `"lts"` and confirm the environment starts with its data intact.
6. Set `mariadbVersion` to `"10.12"`, which does not exist, and run `wp-env start`. It should stop with an error naming `mariadb:10.12`.
7. Set `WP_ENV_MARIADB_VERSION=LTS` and run `wp-env start`. It should fail with a clear validation error naming the variable. Do the same with `WP_ENV_PHP_VERSION=8.2-apache`.

Tested locally on Apple silicon (Docker 29.8.0): `10.3` and `lts` (new and existing environments) start healthy, and switching an `lts` environment to `10.6` shows the downgrade error, then starts again on `lts` with its data intact. `wp db check`, `wp db query` and `wp-env reset` work on `10.3`, on `10.6` with `phpVersion` `7.4` (an older CLI image and client), and on `lts`. `10.12` shows the missing image error, and a start that fails because of a port already in use shows Docker's own error. The health check command was also run directly against the `10.1`, `10.2`, `10.3`, `10.4`, `10.5.8`, `10.6.4`, `10.6`, `10.11`, `11.1.2`, `lts` and `latest` images, including volumes created by older versions, and `10.6.4` on a volume created by `10.6`. Unit tests: `npm run test:unit -- packages/env test/integration/wp-env-schema.test.js`.

## What?

Fixes [Trac #63568](https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/63568) / [#70426](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/70426)

Use quoted and escaped strings for `@font-face` `font-family` values of uploaded fonts.

The problem was that the REST API request was made with a plain string for the `font-family`, whereas the backend expects a string containing CSS text. Something like `WordPress' font` is _invalid_, it is unquoted (not a CSS string) the unescaped `'` would _start_ a CSS string.

With this change, arbitrary font names from uploaded fonts are likely to work well. The font family name is transformed into a CSS string with a number of CSS Unicode escape sequences to remove characters that are often problematic for other parts of the application like KSES or font normalization.

## Why?

The REST API call was made incorrectly, providing a plain string instead of a string containing CSS text. This caused fonts with names containing special characters (e.g. `O'Reilly Sans`) to produce invalid CSS and break the fonts or more CSS on the site.


## How?

- **`createCssString()`** — New function that produces a properly quoted, Unicode-escaped CSS string, neutralizing characters problematic in CSS and WordPress HTML contexts.
- **`CSSStyleSheet` instead of `FontFace` API** — Font faces are now inserted as `@font-face` rules into managed `adoptedStyleSheets`, giving full control over CSS output. `loadFontFaceInBrowser` is now synchronous.
- **Separated display name from CSS value** — New `FontFileMetadata` type carries the raw `fontDisplayName` (for UI/slugs) separately from the escaped `fontFamily` (for CSS).

The `FontFace` API was very problematic because of its inconsistent behavior across browsers. It also expects a "plain" `font-family` string, which made it more difficult to use with the CSS `font-family` that the rest of the WordPress Font API expects to use. The `family` of a `FontFace` instance has inconsistent normalization and is not a CSS string, making it very difficult to compart correctly when attempting to unload a font face.

An E2E test is added with a problematic font name `"Ephesis" font with <special \> {chars} & things, ya'know?` to confirm it's working well.

## Testing Instructions

1. Site Editor > Styles > Typography > Manage Fonts > Upload. (`/wp-admin/site-editor.php?p=%2Fstyles&section=%2Ftypography`)
2. Upload a font with a single quote in its name (e.g. "O'Reilly Sans" from [Trac #63568](https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/63568)). This PR also includes a font that can be used for testing at `test/e2e/assets/Ephesis-modified-name.ttf`. It has more and different special characters.
3. Assign to an element, save, reload — font should persist.
4. Check frontend — font should render.
5. Verify a normal font still uploads and works correctly.

Check for any regressions:

- Try using fonts provided by a theme, like `Fira Code` and `Manrope` in twentytwentyfive.
- Try various Google Font installations and ensure that they continue to work correctly.

## Known issues

I discovered some issues with font display name and font`-family` that are edge cases that should not impact the font's behavior. These are related to some sanitization that was introduced in https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/58636.

### The expected `font-family` is incorrectly sanitized by the REST API (these are the decoded values):

```diff
-"Ephesis" font with <special \> {chars} & things, ya'know?
+"Ephesis"font with <special \>{chars}&things,ya'know?
```

This is incorrect, although it _may_ be harmless. It appears to be the result of [`sanitize_text_field()`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/sanitize_text_field/) stripping "extra" whitespace. This could be addressed in this PR by Unicode escaping carriage returns, line feeds, horizontal tabs, and spaces but that seems excessive. The collapsing of multiple spaces to a single space should maintain correct Unicode escapes, but it means that the following whitespace disappears because it is consumed by the Unicode escape: `\3E  following text` becomes `\3E following text` which is decoded as `>following text` instead of the expected `> following text`. Because the font-family mostly just needs to match, this issue should not be critical although it is worth addressing in follow-up work.

### Font display names are also sanitized in a destructive way.

Font families are stored in a `wp_font_family` post type, where the font family name is stored in the post title. JSON is stored in the post content.

[The family name is sanitized, so a family name is changed:
](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/003664e2ddd20ec053f995c0c2927ee7f2435f9a/src/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-font-families-controller.php#L329-L335)
```diff
-"Ephesis" font with <special \> {chars} & things, ya'know?
+"Ephesis" font with {chars} & things, ya'know?
```

The family name could be stored without additional sanitization in the JSON instead of the post title.

Various AI tools were used for PR feedback.

resources.body:
## What?

Closes #31112

Makes the Query Loop block's taxonomy filters browsable. When you open the Categories field (or Tags, or any other taxonomy), it now lists the existing terms. Before, you had to remember and type a term name before anything appeared.

The controls move from `FormTokenField` to `SearchableChipSelectControl` from `@wordpress/ui`.

## Why?

From the [fifth FSE Outreach Program call for testing](https://make.wordpress.org/test/2021/04/14/fse-program-testing-call-5-query-quest/), two separate testers reported the same thing:

> When selecting the category of the Query block, it would be nice to be able to select from a list of existing categories instead of suggestions from input. Because I do not remember all the categories.

`FormTokenField` only requested terms after the user typed, so you could not reach a term if you did not know its name.

The component choice follows https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/64086#issuecomment-5525387401, which named `SearchableChipSelectControl` as the closest replacement.

## How?

All in `packages/block-library/src/query/edit/inspector-controls/taxonomy-controls.jsx`. Hierarchical and flat taxonomies load their terms in different ways, like the post editor does.

- **Hierarchical taxonomies (Categories).** The whole term tree is loaded in one go (`per_page: -1`, `_fields: 'id,name,parent'`), like the post editor's hierarchical term selector. The list is filtered in the browser.
- **Flat taxonomies (Tags).** These can be very large, so they are searched on the server, like the post editor's flat term selector. With no search, up to 100 terms are listed. A search returns up to 20. The search waits 250ms after typing. Until the new results arrive, the previous results stay on screen, filtered in the browser to match what was typed.
- **Hierarchy.** A nested term shows the names of all the terms above it, like `2023 › Sports`, as the item's `description`. It shows under the name in the list, in a smaller and lighter style, and is the option's accessible description. Chips show it after the name, smaller and lighter, and are named like `News (2023 › Sports)` for screen readers. This way, two terms with the same name can be told apart, even when their parents also have the same name.
- **Include and exclude.** A term that is selected in one control is hidden from the other control. This happens in the browser, so selecting a term does not reload the other control's list when it isn't searching. To make up for the hidden terms, the list asks the server for that many extra terms, up to the REST API limit of 100.
- **Loading.** Terms are only requested when the control is first opened, or when terms are already selected. `statusContent` shows a spinner and "Loading…" while a request is running, and after that a visually hidden result count, following the component's [async example](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-form-searchablechipselectcontrol--docs#async-items). When the server has more matching tags than it returned, `statusContent` says so instead: "Showing 20 of 57 results. Refine your search to see more." when searching, or "Showing the first 100. Search to find more." when browsing, following #84077. `emptyContent` is `null` while loading, because `Combobox.Empty` is a live region and would otherwise announce "No results found." too early.
- **Keyboard.** After typing, the first matching term is highlighted, so <kbd>Enter</kbd> selects it. While the list is still loading and nothing is highlighted, <kbd>Enter</kbd> is ignored, so the typed text is not lost.
- **Announcements.** Adding or removing a term is announced to screen readers, for example "Category added" or "Tag removed". This uses the same strings as the post editor.
- **Selection.** `value` is updated right away when a term is selected. If you select a second term before the first one has loaded, the first one is not lost.

Stored data does not change: plain term ids in `taxQuery.include` / `taxQuery.exclude`. Ids that no longer belong to a real term are still removed, as before.

`getTermIdByTermValue()` is removed. It turned typed text into a term id. The new control works with items, so nothing uses it any more.

Not addressed here: after typing a search, selecting an item closes the popup. Base UI does this whenever the input has text and is outside the popup. So it happens in any `SearchableChipSelectControl` with an outside input. The post editor's Tags field does the same on trunk.

### Trade-offs

- A Tags search does not trim the text, so `news ` with a space at the end finds nothing.
- If more than 100 tags are selected, the chips do not show. The request for them asks for more than the REST API limit of 100. This should be rare.
- In Categories, only the term's own name is searched, so typing a parent's name does not show the terms under it.
- Both the include and the exclude control announce "Category added", not "Category excluded".
- If terms are already selected, the whole category tree loads as soon as the block settings show, not only when the control is opened.
- A very large category tree loads slowly, 100 terms per request. The post editor has the same cost.
- Hierarchical and flat taxonomies have two code paths in the same component.
- The Tags list can show a few less than 100 terms, because terms selected in the other control are hidden in the browser.
- The "of N" total can be slightly too high when a term selected in the other control matches the search but was not in the returned page.
- Tags chips are rebuilt a bit more often than needed.

## Testing Instructions

1. Create several categories:
    - two with the same name under different parents (for example `News` under both `Sports` and `Technology`),
    - two `News` terms one level deeper (for example `2023 › Sports › News` and `2024 › Sports › News`),
    - one with an ampersand (`Q&A`).
2. Create a few tags.
3. Add a Query Loop block to a page, select it, and turn on **Taxonomies** from the ⋮ options menu in the **Filters** panel.
4. Click **Categories** **without typing anything**. The existing categories are listed. This is the fix.
5. Check that the nested `News` terms show `Sports`, `Technology`, `2023 › Sports` and `2024 › Sports` under the name in the list, and after the name in a smaller, lighter style in the chips. Check that they still do when you type `News`.
6. Check that `Q&A` shows a normal `&`.
7. Select several terms quickly, one after the other. All of them should stay selected.
8. Open **Tags** and type part of a tag name. The matching tags should stay in the list while the search loads.
9. Select a term in **Categories**. Check that **Exclude: Categories** does not list it. Check that the block still filters correctly, and that reloading the page keeps the selection.
10. Create more than 100 tags (`npm run wp-env -- run cli wp term generate post_tag --count=120`). Open **Tags** without typing and check for "Showing the first 100. Search to find more." Type `Tag` and check for "Showing 20 of 120 results. Refine your search to see more."
11. Select `Tag 1` in **Tags**, then type `Tag 1` in **Exclude: Tags**. There should still be 20 results, without `Tag 1`.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

1. With the Categories field focused, press <kbd>Down</kbd> to open the list without typing.
2. Move with <kbd>Up</kbd> / <kbd>Down</kbd>, select with <kbd>Enter</kbd>, close with <kbd>Escape</kbd>.
3. Type part of a term name and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. The first matching term is selected.
4. <kbd>Tab</kbd> to a chip's Remove button and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd>.
5. With a screen reader on, check that adding and removing a term is announced.

## Screenshots or screencast

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6b74cd49-c9f3-4b8b-bff5-9e87a8fd3cca

## Use of AI Tools

This PR was authored with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5). The design was decided interactively — scope, the browse limit and ordering, lazy fetching, and how to convey hierarchy were chosen by me at decision points rather than by the model. The implementation, the e2e tests, and the changelog entry were written by the model under that direction.

Verification I had it perform, and reviewed: each e2e test was confirmed to fail on the unmodified code and pass with the change, rather than only asserting the passing state. Behaviour was exercised in wp-env against seeded categories and tags, including eleven categories sharing the name "Events" under different parents. `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint:js` are clean.

I have reviewed the change and take responsibility for it.

Follow-up to #84028, based on [Mirka's suggestion](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84028#discussion_r4182653959) and [the agreement to use maximum-width presets across item popups](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84028#discussion_r4184569508).

This draft is stacked on #84028.

## What?

Add `width` presets to `Menu.Popup`. Change the existing `sm`, `md`, and `lg` item popup presets to size to content up to a maximum width. This also updates Select, Combobox, Autocomplete, and their select wrappers.

## Why?

Short labels should not force a popup to fill the preset width. Maximum widths provide consistent bounds while allowing popups to size to their content.

## How?

Reuse the shared width helper for Menu. Menu defaults to `sm`, retaining #84028's 320px maximum and its existing 160px minimum. Each submenu keeps its own default. Existing Menu CSS overrides still work, and form popups keep their anchor-width minimum.

The existing form presets change behavior. Consumers that need a fixed width can set it with `className` or `style`. Update the prop documentation and add Menu and Select width examples and browser coverage.

## Testing Instructions

1. In Storybook, open **Components / @wordpress-ui / Menu / Popup widths**. Open the menu and try `sm`, `md`, and `lg`. Toggle `longLabels`: short content should use less than the preset width, while longer content can grow up to the cap.
2. Open **More actions** and check that the submenu uses the selected preset. The **Default** Menu story should retain its 320px maximum for root menus and submenus.
3. Open **Components / @wordpress-ui / Form / Primitives / Select / Popup widths**. Repeat the preset and label checks. The popup should stay at least as wide as its trigger.
4. Narrow the viewport and check that Menu stays within the available width.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

Tab to each story's trigger and press Enter. Use the arrow keys to move through items. In Menu, press ArrowRight on **More actions** to open the submenu. Escape should close the popup and return focus to its trigger.

>
> Fixes https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/84058
>
> Adds a search field and filters at the top of the "All notes" sidebar, under the heading and above the thread list:
>
> - **Search** matches the text of a note and its replies (case insensitive, markup ignored).
> - **Status**: All, Open, or Resolved.
> - **Author**: matches threads where the person wrote the note or any reply. Only shown when more than one person has left notes.
>
> When nothing matches, the sidebar says "No notes found." instead of showing the new note form. The floating notes are unchanged.
>
> ## Why?
>
> Once a post has a lot of notes, the sidebar is hard to scan. This gets more pressing as Suggestion mode (#73411) adds more entries to the same list.

> ## How?

> - A new `notes-filters.tsx` holds the controls (`SearchControl` and `SelectControl` from `@wordpress/components`) and a pure `filterNotes()` helper.

Those only exist once Suggestion mode lands, so they are left out here. Adding them later should only mean extending the options and the `filterNotes()` check.

See #80405.

## What?

Adds temporary, side-by-side neutral and brand focus-style comparisons for `@wordpress/ui` Menu, Select, Combobox, and Autocomplete in **Design System → Experiments → Composite focus**. This draft explores the design before changing component defaults.

## Why?

Compare a stronger brand highlight with a lighter neutral highlight, while keeping hover, keyboard focus, virtual focus, and selection distinct.

## How?

Mouse interaction shows the chosen background with its paired foreground. Keyboard navigation shows a focus ring without a background highlight. Combobox and Autocomplete also offer a `virtualIndicator` control to compare that item ring with a side marker plus background highlight. The input retains its focus ring, and checkmarks still identify selected values.

Both highlight treatments use the Button token pairs: solid brand for brand, and hovered minimal neutral for neutral. Hint text and selection indicators use the same foreground when highlighted. Overrides and interaction tracking are scoped to these stories.

## Testing Instructions

1. Run `npm run storybook:dev` and open **Design System → Experiments → Composite focus**.
2. Open each neutral and brand example. Hover items and check the text, hints, and checkmarks against each background. Pointer interaction should show no item ring or side marker.
3. In Combobox and Autocomplete, compare `virtualIndicator: marker` with `ring`. The marker includes the highlight. The ring leaves the row unfilled.
4. Try light, dark, and custom themes with the Theme toolbar. One useful custom sample is primary `#608010` and background `#4f386e`.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

1. Tab to each trigger or input, open the popup, and navigate with arrow keys. Menu and Select show a ring without a highlight.
2. In Combobox and Autocomplete, check that the input retains focus while the active option uses the chosen virtual indicator. Typing still filters the list.
3. Use Enter to choose an option and Escape to dismiss. In Combobox, move away from the selected option and check that the checkmark and active indicator convey different states.
4. Switch between keyboard and mouse interaction. Item rings and markers should disappear when using the pointer, while the highlight remains.

<details>
<summary>Assessment and verification</summary>

I prefer the neutral highlight. It is less visually dominant in a popup, and avoids making each hovered option resemble a primary action. Both options retain matching foreground/background tokens, including hint text. Sampled highlight text contrast was 4.92:1 brand and 14.24:1 neutral in light mode, 5.57:1 brand and 12.94:1 neutral in dark mode, and 4.59:1 brand and 7.64:1 neutral with the custom sample above. These samples do not prove every possible theme.

For editable Combobox and Autocomplete, I prefer the side marker plus background. The input ring identifies where typing goes; the marker identifies the option that arrow keys and Enter act on. Two rings can convey that information, but compete visually. [APG describes retaining DOM focus on the combobox and moving assistive-technology focus with `aria-activedescendant`](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/#listbox-popup-keyboard-interaction). It does not prescribe two visible rings.

The marker uses the paired foreground so it contrasts with either highlight, rather than assuming the focus-ring color contrasts with a brand fill. Ring-only navigation deliberately looks the same in the neutral and brand columns.

Production adoption still needs a design decision, component-local interaction handling, and checks in legacy components and composed consumers such as List View. This draft changes no public API or component default.

Validation: Gutenberg build, Storybook build, Storybook typecheck, focused JS/CSS lint, and browser checks of keyboard navigation, pointer switching, selection, filtering, hint colors, and computed contrast. Forced-colors styles use system colors but have not been tested on Windows. The existing Storybook theme decorator's faded “Themed background” caption triggers a separate contrast violation in themed stories.

</details>

## Use of AI Tools

Codex authored the stories and styles, ran verification, and drafted this description under the author's direction.

Follow-up to [manzoor's suggestion](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/82513#issuecomment-5711737623) on #82513. Related: #83033.

## What?

Rewrite the SVN publisher and its recovery tests as Node scripts.

## Why?

The Bash scripts require GNU `diff` and `timeout`, plus several other shell utilities. Node can handle file copying, comparison, retry delays, and command timeouts directly. Subversion remains the only external tool.

## How?

Use `.mts` scripts with built-in Node APIs and select the repository's Node version in both publication jobs and the SVN test job. The scripts run without installing npm dependencies.

Preserve atomic trunk-and-tag publication, tag-only imports, full-content verification at one revision, bounded read retries, and verification of existing tags. Each publication command runs once; retries only read SVN. Port all existing recovery cases and add checks for binary and symlink differences, filename case differences, invalid options, and symlinked CLI entry points.

## Testing Instructions

1. With the repository's Node version and `svn`/`svnadmin` on `PATH`, run `npm run --workspace @wordpress/release-tools test:svn`.
2. Confirm all 22 checks pass. They use disposable local SVN repositories and require no WordPress.org credentials. Successful publication must verify the complete release; missing, different, unreadable, or mixed-revision contents must fail. A lost commit response must recover without a second write.
3. In CI, confirm `SVN release recovery` succeeds and `Unit Tests - Status Check` waits for it.

<details>
<summary>Validation</summary>

- The original Bash suite passed all 18 checks before conversion. The Node suite passed all 22 checks on Linux, and the existing release-tool suite passed all 173 tests.
- Build, type checking, JavaScript lint, package metadata lint, test routing, and Actionlint workflow checks passed.
- Isolated mutations confirmed that the symlink test fails if comparison follows the target contents, and the stalled-read test fails if the subprocess timeout is removed.
- The filename-case and CLI-entry-point checks passed on macOS and failed against the original Node implementation. Adversarial review found both regressions; both are fixed.

</details>

## Use of AI Tools

Codex implemented the rewrite and tests, performed an independent adversarial review, fixed the findings, and ran the validation above.

resources.body: Potentially an alternative to https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84015. ## What? Refines Menu layout, optimising density. - Items use 8px inline padding by default. - When a menu has radio or checkbox items, the start padding is 4px and labels follow the 16px selection column with no gap, so they start 20px from the item edge. - Checkbox and radio indicators are 16px, matching their column, down from 24px for the checkmark and 20px for the radio. - `Menu.PrefixIcon` renders at 16px by default instead of 24px. The `size` prop still sets a custom size. - Menus and submenus are at most 320px wide (`--wpds-dimension-surface-width-sm`), down from 400px. - Group labels are at least 24px tall, down from 32px. - In a group where only some items have a prefix, items without one are no longer indented to the label column. They start at the prefix column instead, so their labels line up with their siblings' icons. - Descriptions start at the prefix column and run to the item's end padding. Suffixes, shortcuts and submenu chevrons stay centered on the label line instead of the label and description together. - Descriptions sit directly below the label, without the previous 2px gap, and multiple descriptions no longer have extra space between them. - Suffixes and shortcuts render with `Text`'s `body-sm` variant, matching descriptions. - Prefixes use the label color instead of the weaker secondary color, including in highlighted and disabled states. ## Why? Tighter spacing and smaller icons make menus easier to scan and closer to the density of the rest of the admin UI. Aligning unprefixed items and descriptions with the prefix column avoids the staggered left edges that mixed groups produced, so an item reads as one block. Keeping the trailing slots on the label line stops them drifting down on items with descriptions. This drops the previous behaviour where items in a group stayed aligned on the label column even when only some of them had icons. Descriptions need to align with the icon, and keeping that indentation alongside it produced awkward staggered edges. ## How? - `--wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline` is no longer set by default. Both edge tracks read it first and fall back to private defaults: `--_wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline-start` (8px, or 4px with a selection column) and `--_wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline-end` (8px). An override on `Menu.Popup` still sets both edges, with or without a selection column. - The selection gap and indicator size use the existing `--wp-ui-menu-selection-indicator-gap` and `--wp-ui-menu-selection-indicator-size` properties; only their defaults change. - `ItemContent` now renders the label and the descriptions separately. The label is placed directly in the content grid, starting at `prefix-start`, or at `content-start` when the item has its own prefix. Descriptions take a second row of the item grid, always starting at `prefix-start`. - The suffix and shortcut wrappers render `Text` with the `body-sm` variant. Their spacing rules are scoped under `.item-content` so `Text`'s margin reset can't override them when its stylesheet loads later. - The space after descriptions sits on their wrapper rather than on each description, so it appears once, below the last one. - Content still comes before the prefix in the DOM, so Base UI typeahead keeps matching the label text. - Descriptions run to the end of the item rather than stopping before the suffix or shortcut. Stopping them there would need the suffix, shortcut and chevron columns shared across the whole group, which is a larger change. - The editor's Options menu keeps its `width: var(--wpds-dimension-surface-width-sm)` rule, so it fills the menu's maximum width instead of sizing to its longest label. Only the code comment changes. ## Icon stroke width At 16px, the 1.5px stroke of `@wordpress/icons` looks heavy, and the Figma uses a lighter stroke. The icons set `stroke-width` on the root SVG with non-scaling strokes, and there's no supported API to change it, so this PR leaves stroke width alone. A follow-up could add a supported way to set stroke width on icons. ## Impact on consumers - None of the `Menu.PrefixIcon` consumers in the repository pass `size`, so they all move to 16px: the editor Options menu, the DataViews table column header menu and the widget dashboard widget actions. Consumers that need the previous size can pass `size={ 24 }`. - The editor Options menu still renders Dashicon prefixes through `@wordpress/components`' `Icon` at 24px. - Prefix content that is not an icon also takes the label color. - Consumers that set `--wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline`, `--wp-ui-menu-selection-indicator-size` or `--wp-ui-menu-selection-indicator-gap` keep their own values. - Because `--wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline` is no longer set on the popup, a value set on an ancestor now reaches menu items, and CSS that reads the variable's default value gets nothing. No consumer in the repository relies on either. ## Testing Instructions 1. Open the `Menu` stories in Storybook. 2. Check item padding: 8px on both sides with no selection column. With radio or checkbox items, labels start 20px from the item edge. 3. Set `--wp-ui-menu-item-padding-inline` on `Menu.Popup` and check that both edges use it, with and without radio or checkbox items. 4. Check that checkmarks and radio dots are 16px and sit centered on the label line. 5. Check that prefix icons are 16px and match the label color, including when highlighted and when disabled. 6. In a group where only some items have icons, check that items without an icon line up with the icons. 7. Check that descriptions start at the icon column, and that suffixes, shortcuts and chevrons stay centered on the label line. 8. On an item with more than one description, check that the descriptions have no extra space between them. 9. Check that suffix and shortcut text matches the description size, with the usual spacing between label, suffix and shortcut. 10. Check that group labels are 24px tall and line up with item content. 11. Check that a menu with long content stops at 320px wide, and so do its submenus. 12. In the post editor, open the Options menu and check its layout and width. |Before|After| |-|-| | | | | | | ## Use of AI Tools Cursor (Opus 5.5) helped with the implementation and with this description. The changes were reviewed before commit. ## Follow-ups - Add docs about icon usage in groups https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84020 - Add docs about description usage https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84020 - Add higlight to submenu parent items https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84031
