Follow-up to #83089, the optional public lint-defaults step.

## What?

Add `vitest/require-awaited-expect-poll` at error severity to the public `test-unit` config, and allow generated titles passed through variables with `valid-title`'s `allowArguments` option.

## Why?

Floating `expect.poll()` and `expect.element()` assertions currently pass public lint. Gutenberg already enforces this check internally. Generated titles are valid Vitest usage and should not require a repository-specific override.

## How?

Extend Vitest's recommended baseline and remove the corresponding internal overrides. Keep mock-import and other repository conventions internal. Keep a short limitations note in the ESLint README, link to it from the Scripts lint documentation, and put release-specific migration notes below for both packages.

This introduces new lint errors and is recorded under **Breaking Changes** in the Unreleased changelogs of both `@wordpress/eslint-plugin` and `@wordpress/scripts`. Supported dependency ranges and the documented Jest setup stay unchanged.

## Testing Instructions

Run `node tools/validation/test-vitest-consumers.mjs`. It packs the changed tooling into a fresh consumer and checks:

- ESLint 9/10 flat config and ESLint 9's supported legacy wrapper.
- Floating, awaited, and explicitly returned polling and Browser assertions, including the documented helper and aggregation limitations.
- Generated titles, existing callback/promise/title checks, consumer overrides, and the documented Jest lint opt-in.
- The default `wp-scripts lint-js` config for JavaScript and TypeScript tests.

The consumer checks run in the existing Node/Vite CI matrix. Browser runtime behavior is unchanged.

## Migration notes

Published `@wordpress/eslint-plugin` 27.0.0 and `@wordpress/scripts` 36.0.0 do not include these new defaults. This change requires a major release of both packages.

| Entry point | New defaults |
| --- | --- |
| `@wordpress/eslint-plugin` `test-unit` | `vitest/require-awaited-expect-poll` at error severity; `vitest/valid-title` with `allowArguments: true`. |
| Default `wp-scripts lint-js` unit-test config | The same defaults for test/spec files. |

Await `expect.poll()` and `expect.element()` assertions. Helpers can explicitly return the assertion promise if callers await it:

```js
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';

test( 'waits for the result', async () => {
	await expect.poll( () => getResult() ).toBe( 'ready' );
} );

function expectVisible( locator ) {
	return expect.element( locator ).toBeVisible();
}
```

The rule can report valid concise arrow helpers and assertions awaited through variables or `Promise.all()`. See the [unit-test assertion limitations](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/HEAD/packages/eslint-plugin/README.md#unit-test-assertion-limitations) for how to handle those reports without changing the test behavior. The rule does not require Gutenberg's test setup.

Consumers can override either default in a configuration after the preset. Use the `vitest/` namespace in flat config and `@vitest/` in the deprecated ESLint 9 eslintrc wrapper. ESLint 10 supports flat config only. Literal titles still receive validation; generated titles passed through variables are allowed. Gutenberg's mock-import, filename, assertion-helper, and other repository conventions remain internal.

Part of #82293.

Split out of #82480, following @aaronrobertshaw's suggestion to do this per block so each one can be tested and reverted independently.

## What?

Replace the deprecated `word-break: break-word` in the Media & Text block with `word-break: normal` + `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, and remove the Stylelint suppression covering it.

- `packages/block-library/src/media-text/style.scss` — the content column

## Why?

`word-break: break-word` is deprecated. Per CSS Text 3 it is defined as `word-break: normal` plus **`overflow-wrap: anywhere`** — not `overflow-wrap: break-word`. Both halves are set explicitly, so an inherited value such as a theme's `word-break: break-all` cannot change how the content column wraps.

The `anywhere` half matters because the content column is a grid track, so its width comes from intrinsic sizing. With `break-word` the column measured 475px instead of 323px at a 1280px viewport, pushing the media column narrower; `anywhere` preserves the current split exactly.

## How?

Straight declaration swap.

Measured the content column at 375px, 600px, 1024px and 1280px against both candidates. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` reproduced the current geometry at every width; `overflow-wrap: break-word` changed it at every width.

Verification screenshots — front end at two viewports, the editor, and a theme-level `word-break: break-all` compared against trunk — are in the comment below.

## Testing Instructions

1. Add a Media & Text block with a long unbroken string (a long URL works) in the content column.
2. Confirm the text wraps and the media/content split is unchanged, in the editor and on the front end.
3. Narrow the viewport to ~375px and confirm the block stacks and the page does not scroll horizontally.
4. Add `.wp-site-blocks { word-break: break-all; }` as Additional CSS and confirm the content column still wraps on word boundaries while surrounding paragraphs break mid-word.
5. Run `npm run lint:css` — no violations in the changed file.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb50ad9a-7396-48b3-a95a-87a1778acdcf

## What?

An exploratory "browse mode" for the home of the extensible site editor (itself behind the `gutenberg-extensible-site-editor` experiment — so yes, an experiment on top of an experiment).

For block themes, the home canvas is now a live, navigable view of the site's front end with a browser-style address bar. Users browse to the thing they want to change, then click Edit.

## Why?

Users regularly struggle with the difference between content and templates. WordPress often renders views that have no associated page at all (archives, search results, the 404 view, the latest posts home) and resolves them to a template instead. Templates are a far more complex concept than pages, and today the only way to edit one of these views is to work out which template in the hierarchy renders it, find it in the Templates list, and open it. That is confusing and often difficult, even for experienced users.

Browse mode meets users at a location they already know: their website. Instead of asking "which template do I need?", the editor answers it for them. Whatever they are looking at, the address bar tells them what it is and the Edit button takes them to it.

One thing I didn't include but could definitely see working is making the url bar interactive, so that users can search for specific entities to browse/edit.

## How?

**Preview context (PHP).** `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/site-preview.php` adds a `wp_site_preview=1` request mode for users who can `edit_theme_options`. In this mode the admin bar is hidden and a JSON blob describing the current view is printed in the footer: the public URL, the template that rendered it, and — for singular views of an editable, REST-enabled, viewable post type — the post. The posts page is deliberately treated as template-only, because its only editable content is its title.

**Home canvas (`routes/home`).** For block themes, `route.canvas()` returns `null`, so the route renders its own `canvas.tsx`. Classic themes keep the existing preview canvas.

- The iframe loads the front end in preview mode. Same-site links keep the preview flag, off-site links open in a new tab, and admin or login links are left alone.
- The address bar shows an entity icon (post, page, or template), the URL, and a badge naming the entity, e.g. "Page: About" or "Template: Blog Home".
- A single primary button edits the most specific entity: "Edit post", "Edit page", or "Edit template". When a view has both content and a template, "Edit template" moves into a "More actions" menu along with View (opens the URL in a new tab).
- Edit links come from the boot store's `getEntityLink`, so custom post types work through the generic `/types/{type}/edit/{id}` route.
- The previewed location is stored in the route's `preview` search param (e.g. `/?preview=/about/`). Going back from the editor restores the page you were viewing, the URL can be reloaded or shared, and the Home navigation item resets the preview to the site home.

**Boot.** On mobile, the navigation drawer was only offered over preview canvases. It's now also offered over a route's custom canvas when the route has no stage, which this home needs.

**A note on components.** The address bar uses `Button`, `DropdownMenu` and `MenuItem` from `@wordpress/components`. The `@wordpress/ui` equivalents (`Button`, `IconButton`, `Menu`) are flagged by `@wordpress/use-recommended-components` as not yet recommended for WordPress code, so this uses `@wordpress/components` for now and should move over once those components are recommended.

**v1 parity.** This is intentionally v2-only. Browse mode is an exploration of how the extensible site editor's home could work, not a feature to mirror into `packages/edit-site`.

## Testing Instructions

1. Enable the extensible site editor experiment (Gutenberg > Experiments) and activate a block theme such as Twenty Twenty-Five.
2. Open the extensible site editor home (`wp-admin/admin.php?page=site-editor-v2`).
3. Confirm the front end loads with an address bar showing the site URL, a "Template: …" badge, and an "Edit template" button.
4. Click through to a page. The badge reads "Page: <title>", the button reads "Edit page", and "More actions" contains View and Edit template.
5. Click a post, then an archive (category, tag, or author). Check the badge and button update to match each view.
6. Click "Edit page" and confirm the page editor opens. Use the editor's back button and confirm you return to the same page in the preview.
7. Click Home in the main navigation and confirm the preview returns to the site home.
8. From "More actions", check that View opens the current URL in a new tab, and Edit template opens the template that renders the view.
9. Reload the editor while previewing a page and confirm the same page is still shown.
10. Narrow the viewport to mobile width and confirm the navigation menu button is available above the preview.
11. Switch to a classic theme and confirm the home still shows the existing preview.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

1. On the home, tab past the navigation into the address bar and confirm focus reaches the Edit button and then "More actions".
2. Press Enter on the Edit button and confirm the editor opens.
3. Open "More actions" with Enter or Space, move between items with the arrow keys, activate one with Enter, and confirm Escape closes the menu and returns focus to the toggle.
4. Tab into the iframe and confirm links inside the site can be followed with Enter, and that the address bar updates.

## Open questions

- **Template context in the editor.** When a user clicks "Edit template" from a contextual view, such as a specific author's archive, should the template's blocks show that context while they edit? The Query Loop, Archive Title and similar blocks would render that author's posts and name rather than generic placeholder content. That would make the jump from "what I was looking at" to "what I'm editing" much smoother, but it raises questions: it may hide the fact that the template applies to all authors, and the editor would need a way to carry the context in and show it.
- **Custom post type icons.** Posts use the `post` icon, and every other post type falls back to `page`. Post types probably need a way to declare their own icon here.
- **Edit labels for custom post types.** These read "Edit %s" using the post type's singular label as registered (e.g. "Edit Product"), which doesn't follow sentence case.
- **The posts page.** It's treated as template-only, since its only editable content is the title. Is that the right call?

## Use of AI Tools

This PR was written with Claude in Cursor, under my direction and review.

> [!NOTE]  
> The visual design (and probably the code) are all rough, and can be polished if we like the UX.

## What?
Closes #74230.
Alternative to #74283.
Related to #83998.

Adds a `wp:action-trash` link to post and comment REST responses in edit context when the current user can move the record to the trash. `PostTrash` reads it: without the link, it offers "Delete permanently", calls `trashPost( { force: true } )`, and redirects to the list on the new `permanently-delete` action. Before, with trash disabled, the button still said "Move to trash".

## Why?
The client can't tell whether a record can be trashed; only the server knows `EMPTY_TRASH_DAYS`, `MEDIA_TRASH`, and the `rest_{$post_type}_trashable` / `rest_comment_trashable` filters. Sending `DELETE` without `force` for such a record hits core's `rest_trash_not_supported` branch. Notes need the same signal to decide whether a delete can offer Undo, which is why comments are covered too.

## How?
Follows the existing `wp:action-*` links (`action-publish`, `action-sticky`) that the editor already reads from `getCurrentPost()._links`; an editor setting was rejected in #74230 because it isn't entity-scoped. The link is added via `rest_prepare_{$post_type}` and `rest_prepare_comment` filters in `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2`, mirroring the checks in core's `delete_item()`. Menu items, font families, and font faces are skipped because their controllers only support force delete.

## Testing Instructions
1. Add `define( 'EMPTY_TRASH_DAYS', 0 );` to `wp-config.php`.

Spinoff from #83941 that fixes a little bug in the `getMeasurementRender` helper introduced in #80425.

In React 19, elements have refs as part of props, i.e., on `element.props.ref` instead of the old-style `element.ref`. (It's part of the `forwardRef` deprecation project and also one of reasons why React 19 elements are incompatible.) `getMeasurementRender` treats the `ref` incorrectly and now with React 19 it starts to matter.

`sanitizeElement` clears the incoming `ref` to `null`, so that the measurement render doesn't assign to it. But when the `ref` is present on the element, it sets it to `undefined`. The meaning is very different for `cloneElement`. `null` means "reset the ref", `undefined` means "copy the original". So, the ref clearing doesn't work. This PR fixes that by removing `ref` from `isBehaviorProp`.

Then we also don't want to pass the `ref` to the `render` function. Therefore, `getMeasurementProps` must not return it. Because we removed `ref` from `isBehaviorProp`, we need to remove it explicitly.

Two more little nits:
- is the `TRender` type parameter really OK? It allows anything. Should it be more constrained, maybe `extends` from something?
- `enforceRenderProps` and `sanitizeElement` functionality overlaps a lot. Removes `tabIndex` or `aria-current`. The only really specific thing is managing the `href` prop.

## What?

Clarify Tooltip labeling guidance and add an explicit component-purpose check to the Design System UI review skill.

## Why?

We are still occasionally seeing tooltip misuse, so this is an attempt to tighten the documentation and review skill a bit more.

## How?

- Add a checklist item for components used outside their documented purpose. Compare new uses and changed compositions with Storybook guidance or package documentation, separately from prop support and accessibility.
- Recommend the same wording for the tooltip label and trigger's accessible name, with a concrete "Publish" example and a separate keyboard shortcut.
- Explain that visible text, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-label` can provide the accessible name, and that `IconButton` shares its `label` between the accessible name and tooltip.
- Remove the exception for non-critical descriptions and clarify the Popover decision rule. Descriptions, instructions, disabled reasons, and status messages belong outside the tooltip.

## Testing Instructions

1. Read `packages/ui/src/tooltip/stories/usage-guidelines.mdx`. Confirm the label-matching guidance, accessible-name sources, keyboard shortcut exception, and alternatives are consistent.
1. Read `.agents/skills/design-system-ui-review/SKILL.md`. Consider a tooltip used for a disabled reason or dynamic status message and check that the checklist item directs the reviewer to compare that purpose with the usage guidelines, even when the trigger has an accessible description.

Follow-up to #78808.

## What?

Experiment with proportional stroke scaling across the icon library. A 1.5-unit stroke now renders at 1px for a 16px icon, 1.25px for a 20px icon, and 1.5px for a 24px icon.

## Why?

Small icons can look too heavy when their strokes stay at 1.5px. This draft lets us assess native SVG scaling at small and large sizes before deciding whether to adopt it.

## How?

Remove `vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke"` from 339 SVGs, update collection validation and authoring guidance, add browser regression coverage and a size-comparison story, and regenerate the nine affected snapshot files. Keep the existing drawings and stroke-width values.

The Icon block still handles older and custom registered SVGs through its existing scaling override. SVG sanitization continues to support their attributes.

## Testing Instructions

1. Open **Design System → Icons → Icon → Stroke Scaling** in Storybook. Compare the icons at 16, 20, 24, 36, and 48px. Stroke width should scale with size; 24px should look unchanged.
2. Check the existing icon-library story and editor controls, including small menu icons. Compare with trunk for weight, sharpness, and optical balance. Check both standard and high-density displays.
3. Insert an Icon block and resize it. Stroke scaling should match its existing behavior.
4. Try a consumer `strokeWidth` override. The value remains in viewBox units and scales with the icon.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

Use Tab and Enter to navigate the Storybook stories and editor controls. The new comparison is a static table with no new interactive controls.

<details>
<summary>Validation</summary>

- Full build, type checking, and Storybook build passed.
- 35 focused library and Icon-wrapper tests passed. The new validation and browser cases fail against the old behavior.
- All 64 tests in the nine affected snapshot suites passed. Snapshot changes contain only removed attributes and the resulting diff-line count.
- JavaScript and Markdown lint, test routing, and Vitest conventions passed.
- Built CommonJS and ESM consumer checks passed.

## What?

We now have [npm v12 available on the build server](https://make.wordpress.org/systems/2026/09/29/installing-npm-v12-on-the-build-server/).

Closes #82328
Closes #74877
Supersedes #82689

Moves the repository to npm v12 and records the supply chain policy the new major requires.

## Why?

npm v12 is a security release: dependency install scripts, git dependencies and remote URL dependencies all become opt-in. The Node.js Release WG [will not bundle it](https://github.com/nodejs/Release/issues/1161#issuecomment-5280655481) on Node.js 22, 24 or 26, so waiting costs another year with the protections off.

## How?

`devEngines.packageManager.version` is the single source of truth since #82235, so CI and the release tooling pick up `>=12.2.0` from the one-line bump.

`allowScripts` denies every dependency that ships an install script, so nothing compiles on install. `.npmrc` adds `strict-allow-scripts`, so an unlisted script fails the install rather than being skipped silently, and refuses local tarballs.

`@wordpress/icons` is the one approval. npm 12 does not exempt workspace lifecycle scripts from `allowScripts` under `install-strategy=linked` ([npm/cli#9982](https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/9982)), so without it `src/library` never generates on install.

`lockfile-version` is removed from `.npmrc` as it is redundant becuase the lockfile contains the version it's currently in and npm v12 switches to v4 when its new features (patch and extension) are used.

## Testing Instructions

1. `npm install --global npm@12`.
2. Remove every `node_modules`, then `npm ci`. The lockfile should be unchanged and `packages/icons/src/library` populated.
3. Confirm each gate fires (the third edits `package.json`):

```bash
npm install --dry-run --no-save github:sindresorhus/is-odd
npm install --dry-run --no-save https://registry.npmjs.org/is-odd/-/is-odd-3.0.1.tgz
npm pkg delete allowScripts.esbuild && npm install --dry-run
git checkout package.json
```

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

N/A, no user interface change.

## Use of AI Tools

Claude Code drafted and verified the changes against clean installs. I reviewed them.

## What?

Follow up to #83847, alternative to #84017. Restores the initial version of #77913, inspired by https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77177#issuecomment-4312640739

Adds a managed VS Code workspace config to the repo:

- `.vscode/extensions.json`: recommended extensions (EditorConfig, PHP Intelephense, ESLint, Prettier, PHPCS, Stylelint).
- `.vscode/settings.dist.jsonc`: workspace settings template (formatters, code actions on save, Intelephense / PHPCS exclusions, `js/ts.experimental.useTsgo`, and the TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier and Stylelint paths).
- `.vscode/tasks.json`: `folderOpen` task that installs the template into `.vscode/settings.json` if a contributor doesn't already have a customised one.
- `tools/monorepo/scripts/install-vscode-settings.mts`: the cross-platform installer script.
- `.gitignore`: adds `/.vscode/settings.json` so the locally-installed copy isn't committed.

The installer is idempotent: it only writes when the existing `settings.json` matches a previous managed copy (detected by the `// This is a managed VS Code settings file.` header), so contributor customisations are never overwritten.

## Why?

Since #83847, Prettier, ESLint and Stylelint are no longer installed in the root `node_modules`, so editor extensions fall back to their bundled versions unless pointed at the workspaces that declare them. Native TypeScript also needs `js/ts.experimental.useTsgo` and `js/ts.tsdk.path`, which no root dependency can provide (see https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84017#issuecomment-5952462861). A managed settings template makes the supported VS Code experience reproducible without adding those dependencies back to the root.

The installer is a small TypeScript script run by Node's type stripping (no dependencies beyond Node built-ins) so it works on Windows, macOS, and Linux without a POSIX shell.

## How?

- The `folderOpen` task runs `npm run install-vscode-settings --workspace @wordpress/monorepo-tools`, which executes [`tools/monorepo/scripts/install-vscode-settings.mts`](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/692f95ee7775464f17be0d03c8deffffe6fc76b3/tools/monorepo/scripts/install-vscode-settings.mts). VS Code prompts the contributor on first open before running the task.
- Task `type` is `shell` (not `process`) because on Windows `npm` is a `.cmd` shim and `process` would fail to resolve it.
- The installer aborts if the template is missing, no-ops if `settings.json` already matches it, aborts if `settings.json` lacks the managed header, and otherwise copies the template.
- The docs describe the managed setup instead of a copyable settings snippet.

**Note:** `@typescript/native` in root is already useless and it doesn't serve any purpose. I will remove it in a follow up PR.

## Testing Instructions

1. Delete any existing `.vscode/settings.json`.
2. Open the repo in VS Code. When VS Code asks whether to allow automatic tasks, allow them.
3. Confirm `.vscode/settings.json` is created and matches `.vscode/settings.dist.jsonc`.
4. Re-open the folder. Confirm the task reports "Managed settings are up to date; no changes needed."
5. Remove the first line of `.vscode/settings.json`, run **Tasks: Run Task → Install VS Code settings**, and confirm it reports "Custom settings file; aborting."
6. Run "Format Document" on a JS file and confirm `parenSpacing` is applied.

### Testing Instructions for Keyboard

N/A, no UI changes.

## Screenshots or screencast

N/A, editor tooling only.

## Use of AI Tools

Drafted with assistance from Claude Code. All changes were reviewed and tested locally before being pushed.

## What?
Closes #49697

Adds a "Files" category to the inserter's Media tab for non-media attachments.

## Why?
- The Media tab only showed images, video and audio from the library.
- PDFs, documents and archives were unreachable, which led to requests to disable the tab.
- "Open Media Library" silently filtered to images, so uploaded PDFs vanished from the grid.
- Design agreed on a single catch-all "Files" category instead of disabling the tab.

## How?
- Adds a `files` core media category querying `media_type: application`, listed last.
- Non-playable items render a grey placeholder with the file name, matching DataViews.
- Selecting a file inserts a File block that reuses the existing attachment.
- Widens the "Open Media Library" picker to `application` and `text` types.
- `registerInserterMediaCategory` now accepts `application` and `text` as `mediaType`.
- Files category is hidden when `core/file` can't be inserted.

## Testing Instructions
1. Upload a PDF to the Media Library.
2. Create a new post and open Inserter → Media.
3. Confirm a "Files" tab appears last and lists the PDF.
4. Click the PDF and confirm a File block is inserted.
5. Click "Open Media Library" and confirm the PDF is visible in the grid.
6. Delete all non-media files and confirm the Files tab disappears.

Part of https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/74865
Backport PR at https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13911

## What?

This PR implements an extensible Fields API on the server. Consumers tap a `fields_api_init` action to register their fields. Two examples ship in this PR:

1. An [e2e test plugin](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/add/fields-api-endpoint/packages/e2e-tests/plugins/fields-api.php) registering fields imperatively in a variety of scenarios: declarative-only fields, fields with JavaScript (script modules), fields with data (REST), fields with CSS.

```php
function gutenberg_test_fields_api_add_field_declarative( $registry ) {
	$registry->register(
		'gutenberg-test-fields-api', // Origin.
		'postType',                  // Kind.
		'page',                      // Name.
		array(
			array(
				'id'            => 'menu_order',
				'type'          => 'integer',
				'label'         => 'Order',
				'description'   => 'Position of the page among its siblings.',
				'enableSorting' => false,
				'filterBy'      => false,
			),
		)
	);
}
add_action( 'fields_api_init', 'gutenberg_test_fields_api_add_field_declarative' );
```

2. [Core's own fields](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/add/fields-api-endpoint/packages/core-fields/src/index.php), registered declaratively from folders of `field.php` files:

```php
function register_core_field_collections( $registry ) {
	wp_register_field_collection( $registry, __DIR__ . '/page' );
}
add_action( 'fields_api_init', 'register_core_field_collections', 0 );
```

## Why?

Part of https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/74865

## How?

**Server**: `fields_api_init` hook, the registry, and the API

- [Gutenberg_Fields_Registry](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/add/fields-api-endpoint/lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/class-gutenberg-fields-registry.php) holds the fields per entity (`kind`, `name`) and its script module. It exposes `register()`, `update()` and `unregister()`.
- The registry only accepts writes while the `fields_api_init` action fires, and it fires that action lazily the first time something reads it. This is because fields are registered based on the post types and supports, so they need to be registered after `init` but before the REST route/script modules are requested.
- [lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/fields-api.php](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/fields-api-endpoint/lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/fields-api.php#L1) wraps the registry in functions and adds `wp_register_field_collection()`, the declarative format: a folder with `index.php` and one subfolder per field whose `field.php` returns the serializable part of that field. See [core-fields/src/page/field.php](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/add/fields-api-endpoint/packages/core-fields/src/page/index.php) for an example.

**Transport**: `/wp/v2/fields` and preloading

- [Gutenberg_REST_Fields_Controller_7_2](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/1ef191cf7810537ee22f61bdd831e33753c1a54c/lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/class-gutenberg-rest-fields-controller-7-2.php#L1) serves `GET /wp/v2/fields?kind=…&name=…`, returning the entity's `fields` plus the `script_modules` that provide their JavaScript parts.
- [lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/preload.php](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/1ef191cf7810537ee22f61bdd831e33753c1a54c/lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/preload.php#L138) adds the matching preload paths per screen.

**Client**: `core-data` → `fields-loader` → script modules

- `@wordpress/core-data` gains a public `getFieldsConfig( kind, name )` selector (plus resolver, reducer and the `FieldsConfig` type) that requests and caches the route.
- `@wordpress/fields-loader`, a new package, exposes `useFields()` for components and `loadFields()` for route loaders and other code outside React. They merge each script module's default export into the fields that came from REST.
- The modules reach the browser through the import map: `_gutenberg_add_field_modules_to_editor_script()` runs on `admin_footer`, reads the registry, and declares every registered module as a **dynamic** `module_dependencies` entry of the `wp-editor` script. Dynamic means the module is listed in the import map but only fetched when the loader imports it.

**Core's fields**: `@wordpress/core-fields`

- A new package holding every field definition, PHP for the serializable part and TypeScript for the rest, structured per entity: `attachment`, `page`, `wp_template`, `wp_template_part`, `wp_block`.
- We also register (see `post_type_supports` folder) the default fields for every REST-exposed post type from what that post type/theme supports. This serves to bootstrap the fields. A post type can opt out of a registered default field using the `fields_api_post_type_supports_exclusions` filter ([example](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/1ef191cf7810537ee22f61bdd831e33753c1a54c/packages/core-fields/src/index.php#L199)), or just unregister it in `fields_api_init`.

**Screens**

- Every screen has been migrated from `usePostFields` to the new `loadFields()`/`useFields()` utils.
- Some screens still define local fields. Sometimes all of them; some other times in addition to the ones coming from `core-fields`. This table lists all the exceptions so far:

Screen | Local field | Reason
--- | --- | ---

## What changes for consumers

- `wp.editor.registerEntityField` and `wp.editor.unregisterEntityField` are deprecated and **have no effect**. Fields need to be registered in PHP on `fields_api_init` instead.
- The private `usePostFields` hook is gone, and the `core/editor` store no longer holds fields: its private `registerEntityField`, `unregisterEntityField` and `getEntityFields` are gone, and `registerPostTypeSchema` now registers only actions.
- The **format** field comes from the server, offered when the post type supports `post-formats`. Before, it also checked the `disablePostFormats` editor setting, which only the post editor screen set — so it is now hidden consistently in the site editor for themes without post formats.
- The **`content-preview`** field is no longer registered for post types supporting `editor`. No view referenced it; the views that want a preview declare their own.

_I'm going to be away a few days, so I wanted to share how would I do it in case anyone is available/willing to pick it up. Feel free to use your own approach. This can also serve as a map of relationships._

**Stage 1**: prepare, no actual behaviour changes.

*Each can be its own PR, some can be merged together.*

	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/class-gutenberg-fields-registry.php`\
	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/class-gutenberg-rest-fields-controller-7-2.php`
	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/fields-api.php`
	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/preload.php`
	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/rest-api.php`
	- `lib/load.php`
	- All files under `phpunit` but `phpunit/view-config-api-test.php`.
2. Copy `MediaEdit` to media-utils as private API:
	- All files under `packages/media-utils`.
	- Stop re-exporting `MediaEdit` from `@wordpress/fields` (optional, see [thread](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/83368#discussion_r4155039394))
	- `tools/eslint/suppressions.json`.
3. Merge new `core-fields` package:
	- All files under `packages/private-apis/`.
	- All files under `packages/core-fields/`.
	- Verify it doesn't become a global under `wp.*`.
	- Updates to `.github/labeler.yml`.
4. Merge data mechanism:
	- All files under `packages/core-data`.
	- All files under `packages/fields-loader`.
		- Verify the new package doesn't become a global under `wp.*`.
		- Updates to `.github/labeler.yml`.
		- `tools/validation/check-private-apis.config.json`
		- All files under `packages/dependency-extraction-webpack-plugin/`.
5. Fix docs:
	- `docs/private-apis.md`

**Stage 2**: switch consumers.

It can be done one-by-one.

1. Demo plugin
	- All files under `packages/e2e-tests/plugins/fields-api/`.
	- `test/e2e/specs/site-editor/fields-api.spec.js`
2. Site Editor v1
	- All files under `packages/edit-site/` but `packages/edit-site/src/components/sidebar-identity/index.jsx`
3. Media editor:
	- All files under `packages/media-editor`.
	- All files under `routes/media-editor`.
	- `lib/compat/wordpress-7.2/view-config-api.php`
	- `phpunit/view-config-api-test.php`
	- `packages/edit-site/src/components/sidebar-identity/index.jsx`
	- `packages/editor/src/components/media/media-editor-modal.jsx`
	- All fields under `routes/identity/`
4. Site Editor v2
	- All files under `routes/navigation-list/`.
	- All files under `routes/pattern-list/`.
	- All files under `routes/post-list/`.
	- All files under `routes/template-list/`.
	- All files under `routes/template-part-list/`.
5. Editor
	- `packages/edit-post/src/index.jsx`
	- `docs/contributors/code/deprecations.md`.
	- All remaining files under `packages/editor/`.
6. Do not re-export `MediaEdit` from `@wordpress/fields`. (thread)
7. Prevent PRs from being merged into `@wordpress/fields` and `@wordpress/media-fields`. To be decided: lint rule, docs?

**Stage 3**: after WordPress 7.2 release.

1. Deprecate packages `@wordpress/fields` and `@wordpress/media-fields`.

## Testing Instructions

Visit the existing screens and verify they still work as expected:

- Post and page lists, including quick edit and the per-view field controls.
- Templates, template parts, patterns and navigation lists.
- The post summary sidebar in the post editor.
- The media library and the attachment editor form.

## What?
Closes #72515

This PR updates the Site Editor's "Export Theme" functionality to properly separate purely custom, user created templates and template parts from standard theme files. User created files are now routed to `custom-templates/` and `custom-parts/` directories within the exported zip, accompanied by a `CUSTOM-TEMPLATES-README.txt` manifest.

## Why?

With the introduction of the new Template API, there is a strict distinction between default theme templates and custom user generated templates. Previously, custom templates were mixed into the `templates/` and `parts/` directories alongside theme files, or completely ignored. This caused confusion and made it difficult for developers to identify which files were user generated in order to merge them back into their source controlled themes.

## How?

- Introduced `gutenberg_get_template_export_directory()` to classify templates.
    - User created templates go to `custom-templates/` and `custom-parts/`.
    - Theme templates and user edited theme templates stay in `templates/` and `parts/`.
    - Unmodified plugin registered templates are intentionally skipped so they don't pollute the theme export.
- Generates a `CUSTOM-TEMPLATES-README.txt` at the root of the archive outlining how developers can adopt these custom files, including noting which ones need a `customTemplates` entry in `theme.json`.
- Added a full PHPUnit test suite (`Tests_Block_Template_Export`) covering all routing, skipping, and formatting scenarios.

## Testing Instructions

1. Navigate to Appearance > Editor.
2. Go to Templates and create a new Custom Template (e.g., `my-custom-template`). Add a few blocks and save.
3. Go to Patterns > Template Parts and create a new custom template part. Save it.
4. Modify an existing theme template (like Home or Index).
5. Click the Options menu (the three vertical dots) in the top right corner of the Site Editor and click Export.
6. Unzip the downloaded theme file.
7. Verify that the custom template is inside a `custom-templates/` directory, the custom part is inside a `custom-parts/ `directory, and your modified theme template is inside the standard `templates/` directory.
8. Open `CUSTOM-TEMPLATES-README.txt` and verify it correctly lists your custom files and instructions for adopting them.
